title: Why you should STOP doing incline curls
summary: NH explains why he rates dumbbell incline curls as inferior: the fully lengthened bottom is mechanically weak, forces a cheat with the elbows, dictates a mismatched load for the strong mid-range and makes the lift impossible to grind or progress. He contrasts it with preacher curls stopped at 90 degrees and recommends cable incline or behind-the-back cable curls for lengthened training, while stressing that enjoyment and adherence trump all of this.
claims: The incline curl trains the biceps lengthened by letting the arm travel behind the body at the bottom, a stretch other curls don't offer
Rule of thumb for biceps safety: as long as the shoulder is mobile and moves with the arm, the biceps can overextend safely; tears happen when the shoulder is frozen and the arm overextends
Preacher curls can be dangerous because the shoulder is frozen in space; overextending the elbow there loads the biceps tendon
The incline curl is safe because the shoulder stays mobile; its problem is hypertrophy, not injury
At full extension the biceps is disengaged and mechanically weak; tension there is passive, so lifters must swing the elbows forward to build momentum out of the bottom
The elbow-forward swing is proper form on incline curls, but needing it shows the lengthened bottom position is a flaw of the lift
Lengthened-position studies conflict; he cites a recent one with about 100 men where training only around 90 degrees outgrew training only lengthened
The biceps works best and gets most of its stimulus around the 90-degree elbow angle
Because the weak bottom dictates the dumbbell you choose, either the strong 90-degree portion is underloaded or you must cheat the bottom; incline curls get the worst of both
Train lengthened and mid-range separately rather than combining them in one hybrid lift
A good lift lets you grind: reps slow gradually until you are essentially at failure; on incline curls reps stay fast then one rep suddenly dies, so you spend no time near failure
Preacher curls stopped at 90 degrees give constant tension, gradual rep slowdown and let him rest at the top to grind extra reps close to true failure
The uneven strength curve makes incline curls hard to progressively overload; going heavier just means more cheating at the bottom
People keep doing incline curls mainly for the stretch sensation

If you want incline curls, do them on a cable from a bench in the middle of the cable station; the cable resistance profile fixes the strength curve, reduces cheating and allows grinding and progression
Behind-the-back standing cable curls train the biceps lengthened without the dumbbell incline curl's problems
Enjoyment of a lift matters more than its hypertrophy rating because adherence drives consistency; a C-tier lift you love beats an S-tier lift you don't
exercises: elbows swing forward to leave the bottom
big stretch but weak bottom, poor strength curve, hard to grind
stop at 90 degrees, arm parallel to floor; no swinging; rest at top
constant tension, grind to true failure, safe if not overextended
sit on a bench in the middle of the cable station
fixes strength curve of dumbbell version
